trap: Becomes either a fundraising appeal ("give what little you have and watch it multiply") or a bare nature-miracle spectacle — missing that Jesus withdrew in grief first, and that the miracle grows out of sorrow, not showmanship.
hinge: He feeds five thousand from nothing, but through the disciples' hands, not around them — the miracle needs their meager five loaves and the labor of carrying them out, basket by basket.

doors.claim: Even grieving his own loss, Jesus turns toward the crowd's hunger — the compassion is not despite the sorrow but issuing from it.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: He did not retire into the desert through fear of death, as some suppose, but in mercy to His enemies, that they might not add murder to murder.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: He went out and saw a great multitude, and he had compassion upon them, and healed their sick.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Jesus withdrew into a desert place — to avoid Herod; because of the multitude pressing upon him; and to talk with his disciples, newly returned from their progress, apart.

doors.say: He was grieving when he saw the crowd's hunger — and grief did not close his hand, it opened it.
doors.do: Ask them to name one act of compassion they've withheld because they felt too depleted to give it, and give it anyway this week.

doors.landing: Through their hands, not around them
doors.claim: Christ multiplies through the disciples' offering and labor, not instead of it — the miracle needs what little they have and the work of carrying it out.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: Wherein He calls the Apostles to breaking of bread, that the greatness of the miracle might be more evident by their testimony that they had none.

witnesses.author: Hilary of Poitiers
witnesses.reading: Then the loaves are given to the Apostles, because through them the gifts of divine grace were to be rendered.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: He provokes them to give, that, when they testify that they have nothing, the greatness of the sign may be the better known; wherein he also hints that by them the hungry hearts are to be fed.

doors.say: He didn't multiply the bread and hand it out himself — he put it in their hands and sent them into the crowd.
doors.do: Have them identify the meager thing they've been holding back from ministry because it seemed too small to matter, and hand it over.

doors.claim: The twelve leftover baskets testify that nothing of Christ's provision is wasted or forgotten — abundance leaves a record.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: For this reason also He caused twelve baskets to remain over and above, that Judas might bear his basket.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: Each of the Apostles fills his basket of the fragments left by his Saviour, that these fragments might witness that they were true loaves that were multiplied.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: The fragments are not to be held negligently, but diligently sought out by the twelve apostles, who are signified by the twelve baskets, and by their successors. With baskets servile works are carried on.

doors.say: Even the leftovers were gathered up — nothing Christ provides is thrown away, not even the excess.
doors.do: Have the congregation name one thing God provided that they let go to waste, and commit to gathering the fragments this time.

doors.claim: The only qualification Isaiah names is thirst — the ones with no money, and no merit to spend, are the ones called.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: This thirst implies a vehement, and active, and restless desire. No money — those who are most worthless and wicked, if they do but thirst, may be welcome. Buy — procure or receive that which is freely offered.

doors.say: You are not too poor for this table. Thirst is the whole of the admission price.
doors.do: Invite them to name the thing they think disqualifies them from God's table, and to come anyway.

doors.landing: Spending on what does not feed
doors.claim: The prophet's charge is against misdirected hunger: people pour everything into what cannot nourish, and the church can do it with holy words.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Money — all your time, and strength, and cost. Not bread — for those things which can never nourish or satisfy you, such as worldly goods, or pleasures.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: You weigh the sacred words, but not the refreshment. You who keep the appearance of the letter alone lose, from the spiritual understanding, the fatness of the inward refreshment.

doors.say: It is possible to spend a lifetime on things that do not feed you, and to handle Scripture the same way.
doors.do: Ask them to name one place their time and strength go that leaves them hungrier, and to give that hour to the word instead.

complementary.gravity: Isaiah calls everyone who thirsts, even those with no money, to come and buy wine and milk without price (Isaiah 55); the Psalm praises the Lord whose open hand satisfies every living thing; Paul will not stop grieving for kin outside the promise (Romans 9); and Jesus, grieving John's death, feeds a famished crowd from five loaves. The nerve: a table set free for people who arrive with nothing to pay.

synthesis.convergence: Isaiah opens a market where the poor buy without money (Isaiah 55); the Psalm sings of a hand opened to satisfy every living thing (Psalm 145); Paul refuses to stop grieving for the ones outside (Romans 9); and in the wilderness five loaves feed thousands who brought nothing (Matthew 14). Every reading sets God's table for empty hands, and asks why we keep spending ourselves on what does not feed.
synthesis.claim: This bread cannot be bought and does not have to be: come hungry, and bring the little you have to the one who feeds.
synthesis.here: For people spending themselves on what is not bread — overwork, accumulation, earning their place — the move is invitation, not demand: stop paying, and come and eat.

semicontinuous.gravity: Jacob wrestles all night at the Jabbok and limps away blessed (Genesis 32); the Psalm cries out of hunger and want; Paul aches with grief for kin cut off from the promise (Romans 9); and Jesus — grieving John's death — turns from his own sorrow to feed a famished crowd from five loaves. The nerve: compassion answering scarcity in the wake of loss, not around it.

synthesis.convergence: Jacob limps away blessed after wrestling all night (Genesis 32); the crowd waits all day in the wilderness and is fed at evening; Paul aches with grief over kin estranged from the promise (Romans 9). Every reading meets people spent, hungry, or grieving and finds God meeting them there with abundance out of scarcity — through their exhaustion, not around it.
synthesis.claim: God does not wait for your strength to return before feeding you — bring what little you have, spent as you are, and watch it be enough.
synthesis.here: For a congregation running on empty — post-loss, post-crisis, depleted — don't ask them to muster more. Ask them to bring the five loaves they already have and hand it over.

subtract: Three landings — grief turned to compassion, the disciples' hands, or the leftover witness. Choose the one your people most need; let the other two go.
source: Catena Aurea (Aquinas; J.H. Newman tr., public domain), Wesley's Explanatory Notes, and the Glossa ordinaria (Migne recension, Wroot Press English), retrieved from ~/reception-corpus — attested, not authored.
